claims.claim: Early childhood is the developmental period from about age two to about age six; sources vary the borders (CDC milestone checklists run from age two through five; OpenStax Lifespan Development frames the period as roughly ages three to six).
Physical growth slows in early childhood: on average about 2 to 3 inches of height and 4 to 5 pounds of weight per year across ages three to six in the United States.
By age six the brain has reached about 90 percent of its adult size while the body has reached only about 30 percent of adult weight.
The World Health Organization advises that preschool children typically need ten to thirteen hours of sleep per twenty-four hours.
In early childhood, motor skills shift from lumbering, awkward movement toward more adult-like movement; gross motor (whole body) and fine motor (hands and fingers) skills both develop.

CDC typical milestones: most children run easily by about age three, climb onto and down from furniture unassisted by about age two, pedal a tricycle by about three, copy a circle by about three, draw a person with two to four body parts by about four, and copy triangles and print some letters by about five.
CDC typical social milestones: most children take turns in games by about age three and cooperate with other children by about age four.
Jean Piaget's preoperational stage (about ages two to seven) describes thinking that is symbolic and imaginative, with pretend play prominent, but without adult-style logic.

Play in early childhood fosters cognitive development, social skills, emotional regulation, language, and problem-solving; the American Academy of Pediatrics published a clinical report on the importance of play (Ginsburg et al., 2007, as cited in OpenStax).
Individual variation in development is normal; group averages mask large individual differences, and milestones are typical ranges rather than deadlines.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Where early childhood begins and ends
positions: Ages about 2 to 6 (working definition used here; the CDC milestone framework tracks children from age 2 through age 5)
Ages 3 to 6 (OpenStax Lifespan Development chapter framing)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses 'about age two to about age six' as the working definition and explicitly states that sources vary the borders.

conflictingEvidence.issue: CDC milestone wording changes across checklist updates (2009, 2021, 2022 editions differ in wording and some ages)
positions: E.g., stairs milestone phrased 'walks up and down stairs alternating feet' (2009) vs 'walks up and down stairs, one foot on each step' (2021)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states milestones as typical ranges ('most children by about age X') and cites the CDC framework generally rather than one update's exact wording.

positions: U.S. averages: about 2-3 inches and 4-5 pounds per year
Nutrition, genetics, and environment shift individual growth substantially
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Averages are presented as averages, with an explicit note that individual variation is normal (per OpenStax).

sourceRecords.title: 5.1 Physical Health and Growth in Early Childhood — Lifespan Development | OpenStax
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. openstax.org blocks direct fetch, so the section was read via an Internet Archive Wayback capture (2024). Supports: early childhood framing (ages 3-6 in this book), average growth of 2-3 inches and 4-5 pounds per year, brain at ~90% of adult size by age six, body at ~30% of adult weight, WHO sleep guidance of 10-13 hours for preschool children, and the statement that individual variation is normal.

sourceRecords.title: 5.2 Motor Development and Physical Skills in Early Childhood — Lifespan Development | OpenStax
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Internet Archive Wayback capture. Supports: gross vs fine motor distinction, the transition from 'somewhat lumbering, awkward behaviors to more adult-like motor movement,' milestones as indicators of brain development, and WHO physical-activity guidance for this age.

sourceRecords.title: 5.5 Play in Early Childhood — Lifespan Development | OpenStax
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Internet Archive Wayback capture. Supports: play's role in fostering cognitive development, social skills, emotional regulation, language, and problem-solving; play stages (solitary, parallel, cooperative); and the American Academy of Pediatrics clinical report on the importance of play (Ginsburg et al., 2007) cited by the chapter.

sourceRecords.title: CDC's Developmental Milestones — Learn the Signs. Act Early.
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Canonical index URL registered; content read from archived age-specific pages (2, 3, 4, and 5 years) via web.archive.org captures (2009 and 2021-era editions). Supports typical milestones as 'things most children do by these ages': running easily (3), climbing onto/down from furniture unassisted (2), tricycle (3), stairs one foot per step (3), copying a circle (3), drawing a person with 2-4 body parts (4), copying triangles and printing some letters (5), taking turns in games (3), cooperating with other children (4). CDC milestone checklists run from age two through five, supporting the working definition window.

sourceRecords.title: Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development — Simply Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: the preoperational stage as Piaget's second stage occurring between 2 and 7 years, symbolic and pretend play becoming more important, and egocentrism as a feature of the stage. Used only for the one-line Piaget attribution; the stage's full treatment belongs to the cognitive-development topic.
